title: Corporate catering for design studios: a complete guide
body_markdown:
Design studio catering is food service planned around creative work, client meetings and shared studio space, with the aim of feeding people without disrupting the work or presentation. To plan catering for design studios, choose the service format before the menu: a working lunch, client presentation and studio launch need different layouts, staffing and clearing arrangements.


**TL;DR**

- Plan catering for design studios around the meeting format, usable space and responsibility for clearing.
- myCHEF provides corporate catering in Dubai; request a proposal matched to your studio’s event brief.
- Choose boxed meals for individual breaks, buffets for shared lunches and staffed service when hosting takes priority.
- Confirm dietary requirements, building access and collection arrangements before approving the menu.


## Why catering matters for design studios

A studio lunch has to fit the room as well as the guest list. If your meeting table also holds drawings, samples or presentation equipment, food needs a separate landing place. If clients are reviewing work, service should fit around the discussion rather than interrupt it.

**The right format protects your working space and gives someone clear responsibility for hosting.** Start with the occasion: feeding the team, welcoming clients or entertaining guests after a presentation. Those are different briefs, even when the guest count stays the same.

For a corporate catering proposal, use the [myCHEF enquiry page](https://www.mychef.ae/contact) to send your event details and ask which service arrangements fit. myCHEF provides corporate event catering in Dubai; confirm the menu, staffing and practical scope in your proposal rather than assuming they are included.

## How do you plan catering around studio work?

### Define the occasion

Write a short event brief before looking at dishes. State whether people will continue working, sit down together or move between displays and conversations. Then decide what must remain uninterrupted: a client presentation, a review session or access to a shared workbench.

For example, an illustrative lunch for 18 team members and 6 clients starts with 24 people, not a standard package label. Separate those groups if their arrival times or meal requirements differ. Count presenters and external collaborators if they are also eating.

- **Event purpose:** identify a team lunch, client meeting or studio celebration.
- **Guest count:** separate confirmed attendees from unconfirmed invitations.
- **Meeting schedule:** mark the moments when service must pause.
- **Hosting responsibility:** name the person authorised to approve changes.

### Choose the format

Start with a simple floor sketch and a walk through the room. Mark where food can arrive, where guests can collect it and where used dishes will go. A format that fits on paper still needs a workable route through the studio.

Choose individual meals when people need flexibility. Choose a buffet when there is a shared break and a dedicated serving surface. Consider staffed service when your team needs to concentrate on guests rather than replenishing dishes or clearing plates. None of these formats removes the need for an agreed clean-up plan.

- **Individual meals:** assign meals clearly when dietary needs vary.
- **Shared buffet:** reserve space for serving utensils and a queue.
- **Passed bites:** confirm staffing and how substantial the food should be.
- **Seated service:** check seats, table space and access behind guests.

### Build the menu

Draft a menu by function before naming dishes: a main component, a substantial vegetarian alternative, accompaniments and drinks. Then check whether each item suits the way people will eat. Food that needs cutting belongs at a proper place setting, not beside an open laptop.

myCHEF corporate catering is best suited to Dubai businesses seeking an event menu and service brief tailored to their gathering. The trade-off is that you need to agree the scope: the service description alone does not establish what equipment, tableware or staffing your quotation contains.

Collect dietary requirements directly. A vegetarian preference and a food allergy need different information; do not reduce both to a tick beside a menu item.

- **Meal balance:** include a substantial alternative, not only side dishes.
- **Eating position:** match dishes to seated or standing guests.
- **Dietary details:** record requirements against individual attendees.
- **Service method:** confirm how dishes will be labelled and separated.
- **Drinks provision:** assign responsibility for water, cups and replenishment.

### Check the space

Photographs and a measured sketch give a caterer a clearer brief than “small office kitchen”. Show the proposed serving surface, preparation area and route from the entrance. Tell the caterer which surfaces cannot be used, especially where you keep models, material samples or unfinished work.

For a Dubai studio in a managed building, ask your building contact about delivery access, visitor registration, loading arrangements and waste collection. Pass the confirmed arrangements to the caterer. Do not assume access through the main reception also works for food deliveries or equipment collection.

- **Arrival route:** identify the entrance, lift and unloading point.
- **Serving area:** reserve a clear surface away from project materials.
- **Kitchen facilities:** list the facilities actually available for use.
- **Power access:** confirm equipment needs before allocating sockets.
- **Waste route:** agree where packaging and used items will wait.

### Compare the scope

Send the same written brief to each provider you are considering. Ask for the proposal to separate food, delivery, setup, service, equipment and clearing. This makes differences visible without treating every quotation as an identical service.

A menu description is not a staffing plan. Ask who places the food, who replenishes it and who removes used items while your team is hosting. If you are considering myCHEF, request written confirmation of these responsibilities alongside the proposed menu; do not infer them from photographs or dish names.

- **Food quantities:** confirm portions and what constitutes a complete meal.
- **Service roles:** distinguish delivery, setup, serving and clearing.
- **Equipment:** identify supplied items and anything the studio must provide.
- **Dietary handling:** ask how individual meals and shared dishes are identified.
- **Changes:** confirm how guest-count and menu revisions are handled.

### Set the handover

Build the catering schedule around the meeting agenda, working backwards from when guests should eat. Delivery, setup and service are separate milestones. Give each a named contact so the presenter does not become the delivery coordinator halfway through a review.

Agree how the room should look when service ends. “Clear everything” leaves questions about hired equipment, packaging, leftover food and furniture. Record the handover in the event brief and share it with the person opening the studio, not just the person booking the food.

- **Arrival:** assign a contact who can answer the driver or service team.
- **Setup:** confirm when the serving area becomes accessible.
- **Service:** align food presentation with the agreed break.
- **Clearing:** identify what leaves immediately and what awaits collection.
- **Handover:** check the room before the catering contact departs.

The planning sequence is straightforward: define the occasion, choose the format, build the menu, check the space, compare the scope and set the handover. Keeping those decisions separate makes omissions easier to spot.

## Which catering format suits your studio event?

Compare service formats by the job they need to do. These are planning options, not confirmed myCHEF packages; request the exact arrangements you need in your enquiry.

| Option | Best for | Main advantage | Key limitation |
|---|---|---|---|
| Individual boxed meals | Working lunches and staggered breaks | Makes individual distribution straightforward | Packaging and used containers still need managing |
| Drop-off buffet | Team lunches with a shared break | Lets guests choose from a shared menu | Your team needs an agreed setup and replenishment plan |
| Staffed buffet | Client workshops and larger studio gatherings | Assigns service tasks to an agreed team | Needs room for staff movement and serving equipment |
| Passed canapés | Studio openings and standing receptions | Keeps guests free to move and talk | Small bites should not be presented as a full meal without an appropriate menu |
| Plated meal | Seated client entertaining | Gives the meal a defined service structure | Requires suitable seating, tableware and a clear service route |

**Choose the least complicated format that meets the occasion.** Adding service elements without a reason also adds coordination: more equipment to place, more movements through the room and more responsibilities to confirm.

If guests are standing around a materials display, check whether they can comfortably hold the proposed food and a drink. If the event includes a full meal, give that meal enough space and time rather than treating it as an accessory to the presentation.

## What could a studio lunch menu look like?

The following is an illustrative menu structure, not a myCHEF package or a statement of what is available. Use it to explain the balance you want, then ask the caterer to propose suitable dishes.

For a seated working lunch, a possible structure is a chicken main, a substantial chickpea-based vegetarian main, rice, a dressed salad and individual fruit portions. Ask how sauces, utensils and dietary meals will be presented. Choose the final dishes against the confirmed requirements, not the other way round.

For a standing reception, describe the eating conditions first: guests are moving between displays, holding drinks and talking. Ask for bites suited to that setting, plus a clear explanation of whether the overall menu is intended as light refreshments or a meal.

The practical question behind [catering ideas for small offices](https://www.forkandfarmcatering.com/best-catering-ideas-for-small-calgary-business-offices/) is how food service fits a workspace that still needs to function. In a design studio, apply that question to the serving surface, circulation route and protected project area before choosing decorative presentation pieces.

## Which mistakes should design studios avoid?

### Treating a workbench as spare buffet space

A surface is not available merely because nobody is using it at that moment. Confirm permission before moving samples, prototypes or equipment, and nominate a separate place for deliveries. The setup team needs a clear boundary, not an invitation to reorganise the studio.

### Choosing presentation over practicality

An attractive dish still needs to work with the guest’s plate, cutlery and seating. Review the menu against the room: standing guests need a different eating arrangement from clients seated for lunch. Keep sauces and serving utensils away from presentation materials.

### Leaving the presenter in charge of service

The person leading a client review should not also manage arrivals, missing utensils and collection calls. Assign an operational contact who knows the brief and can make small decisions without interrupting the meeting.

### Assuming dietary labels settle every question

A label communicates information; it does not replace a discussion about ingredients and preparation. Share allergies and other dietary requirements before menu approval, and ask the provider to explain what it can accommodate. Never make assurances to a guest that the caterer has not confirmed.

## What should your final catering brief include?

Keep the approved brief short enough for the studio contact to use on the day. Attach the menu and proposal, but put the operational details where they are easy to find. For the illustrative 24-person lunch, that means a confirmed headcount alongside named dietary meals, not just a total copied from the original enquiry.

Include the date, full location, access instructions, service format, meal time and contact details. Add the agreed serving area, equipment responsibilities and collection arrangement. Finish with a clear record of who approves changes.

**A useful brief describes the whole visit, not just the food.** Share the final version with the caterer, the studio host and anyone responsible for building access. Update those people together if the arrangements change.

## FAQ


**What is the best catering format for a design studio lunch?**

Individual meals suit separate breaks, while a buffet suits a shared lunch with a dedicated serving area. Choose staffed service when your team needs to focus on guests rather than replenishment and clearing.

**Can we arrange catering without a studio kitchen?**

Describe the facilities you have and ask the caterer to propose a service method that works without on-site cooking. Confirm preparation, equipment and serving arrangements before approving the menu.

**How do we calculate the guest count for a client presentation?**

Count everyone who will eat, including staff, clients, presenters and external collaborators. Separate confirmed attendees from unconfirmed invitations and agree how changes will be handled.

**What should we tell the caterer about food allergies?**

Share each guest’s stated allergy before menu approval and ask how the provider can accommodate it. Confirm ingredients, preparation and serving arrangements rather than relying on a dietary label alone.

**Does corporate catering include serving staff and cleaning?**

Serving staff and cleaning must be confirmed in the proposal. Ask separately about setup, replenishment, clearing during the event, equipment collection and the final condition of the room.

**What affects a design studio catering quotation?**

Guest count, menu, service format, staffing, equipment and access arrangements define the quotation’s scope. Compare proposals against the same brief and request current figures directly from the provider.

**What information does myCHEF need for a studio catering enquiry?**

Send myCHEF the date, Dubai location, guest count and service required. Add the event schedule, dietary requirements, available facilities and building access details so the proposal addresses the practical arrangements.

- [Serving staff and cleanup for catered events](https://www.mychef.ae/blog/can-catering-companies-in-dubai-provide-serving-staff-and-cleanup)

## Plan the room reset, not just the arrival

Before you approve the catering, ask what happens when the next meeting starts. A studio that needs its main table back immediately has a different clearing brief from one hosting an evening reception. Make that deadline explicit.

To discuss your studio event with myCHEF, send the date, location, guest count and service required through the enquiry page. Include whether guests will be working, seated or standing, and when the space needs to be ready for use again.
